lessons.title: Heap Structure — Min And Max Heap
lessons.objective: Understand the heap property, how a heap is stored in an array using index arithmetic, and why this array-based storage achieves cache-friendly O(log n) operations.
concepts: Heap definition: complete binary tree satisfying the heap property
Min-heap: every parent ≤ both children (root is minimum)
Max-heap: every parent ≥ both children (root is maximum)
Complete binary tree: all levels full except last, filled left to right
Array representation: root at index 1, parent(i)=floor(i/2), left=2i, right=2i+1
0-indexed variant: parent=floor((i-1)/2), left=2i+1, right=2i+2
Why array storage: no pointers, cache-friendly, O(1) index arithmetic
Height of a heap with n nodes: floor(log2 n)
lessons.explanation: A heap is a complete binary tree where every node satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap, every parent is less than or equal to both its children. In a max-heap, every parent is greater than or equal to both children. The heap property guarantees the root is always the minimum (min-heap) or maximum (max-heap). Heaps are stored in arrays without pointers using index arithmetic: for a 1-indexed array, the node at index i has its parent at index floor(i/2), left child at 2i, and right child at 2i+1. For a 0-indexed array: parent at floor((i-1)/2), left at 2i+1, right at 2i+2. This arithmetic maps perfectly onto the complete binary tree structure because a complete tree fills levels left to right without gaps, making array positions contiguous. The array storage gives excellent cache locality since parent and child nodes are nearby in memory. A heap with n nodes has height floor(log2 n), which is why operations touching only the root-to-leaf path cost O(log n).
lessons.analogy: A min-heap is a tournament bracket where the winner (minimum) is always at the top. Every match result satisfies the rule: the winner beats both their children. The array storage is like a numbered seating chart: seat 1 is the root, seat 2 and 3 are its children, seat 4 through 7 are the grandchildren. You never need an address book (pointer) — the seat number tells you exactly where your parent and children sit.

code_example.explanation: The 1-indexed representation (null at index 0) produces cleaner index arithmetic: parent = i/2, left = 2i, right = 2i+1. The 0-indexed variant (parent = (i-1)/2, left = 2i+1, right = 2i+2) avoids the dummy null but has slightly more complex formulas. In interviews, either convention is fine — state which one you are using at the start.

common_mistakes: Confusing 0-indexed and 1-indexed heap arithmetic — using parent=i/2 with 0-indexed gives wrong results for i=1 (parent=0 correct) but wrong for i=2 (parent=1 correct by coincidence); always state and verify your indexing convention
Thinking a heap is a Binary Search Tree — a BST has sorted order between left and right children; a heap only requires parent to be smaller/larger than children, with no ordering between siblings

Forgetting that the heap property only guarantees the root is the extreme value — the second-smallest element in a min-heap may be at index 2, 3, or anywhere in the first two levels; arbitrary access requires O(n) search
lessons.interview_relevance: Interviewers expect you to derive the parent/child index formulas on the spot without memorising them. The derivation: a complete binary tree fills level k from left to right; level k has 2^k nodes starting at index 2^k in a 1-indexed array; the parent of node i is at floor(i/2) because integer division by 2 gives the position in the previous level. Being able to explain this derivation signals genuine understanding.

What are the children of index 2? What is the height? Is this a perfect binary tree? Compute the index arithmetic manually without using the formulas to verify you understand the derivation.

A heap is a COMPLETE BINARY TREE where every parent satisfies an ordering constraint with its children — in a min-heap every parent is LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO both children (root holds the minimum), while in a max-heap every parent is GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO both children (root holds the maximum); critically, the heap property only constrains parent-child relationships, NOT the order of siblings

theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's exact definitions: 'Min-heap: every parent ≤ both children (root is minimum)' and 'Max-heap: every parent ≥ both children (root is maximum)' — the 'complete binary tree' requirement (all levels full except possibly the last, filled left-to-right) enables the compact array storage that makes heaps efficient.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the array-based heap use INDEX 1 as the root (not index 0), and what index arithmetic formulas does this enable?
options: Index 0 is reserved for the array's length; index 1 always holds null

Using index 1 as the root produces especially CLEAN arithmetic: parent(i) = floor(i/2), left(i) = 2i, right(i) = 2i+1 — these simple formulas work because powers of 2 align naturally with 1-indexed positions; with 0-indexing the formulas become parent(i) = floor((i-1)/2), left(i) = 2i+1, right(i) = 2i+2, which is slightly more complex (hence the lesson's choice of [null] as index-0 placeholder)
Index 0 is used for overflow values when the heap is full
JavaScript arrays require index 1 as the first usable slot
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concepts: '1-indexed: parent(i)=floor(i/2), left=2i, right=2i+1' — the 1-indexed convention produces simpler arithmetic that's easier to verify and remember; the `[null]` at index 0 is just a placeholder to enable this cleaner indexing.

Height = ceil(log₂(n)); a 7-node heap has height 3
Height = n/2; a 7-node heap has height 3

lessons.title: Heap Insert And Extract
lessons.objective: Implement heap insert using sift-up and extract-min using sift-down, prove both are O(log n), and build a complete MinHeap class from scratch.
concepts: Insert: append to end (maintain completeness), sift-up to restore heap property
Sift-up: swap with parent while parent > current (min-heap)
Extract min: swap root with last element, remove last, sift-down root
Sift-down: swap with smaller child while current > either child (min-heap)
Both operations: O(log n) — at most height swaps
Heapify (build heap from array): O(n) using bottom-up sift-down
Heapify O(n) proof: more nodes near leaves, sift-down costs less there
Priority queue as heap abstraction
lessons.explanation: Insert adds a new element while maintaining both the completeness property (array representation) and the heap property. Step 1: append the new element to the end of the array (maintains completeness). Step 2: sift-up — repeatedly compare the new element with its parent and swap if the heap property is violated, until it reaches the correct position or becomes the root. At most O(log n) swaps since the tree has height log n. Extract-min removes and returns the root (the minimum). Step 1: swap the root with the last element. Step 2: remove the last element (the old root). Step 3: sift-down the new root — repeatedly compare with both children and swap with the smaller child until the heap property is restored or we reach a leaf. Again O(log n) swaps. Heapify builds a heap from an unsorted array in O(n) by applying sift-down to all non-leaf nodes from bottom to top. The O(n) proof: most nodes are near the leaves and require few swaps; the sum of work across all levels converges to O(n).
lessons.analogy: Insert with sift-up is like a new employee joining a company hierarchy. They start at the lowest position and bubble up if they are more qualified than their manager, swapping positions until everyone above them is more senior. Extract-min is like the CEO retiring: the most junior employee (last in the array) temporarily takes the CEO position, then sifts back down to their appropriate level by comparing with subordinates and swapping with the more capable one.

code_example.explanation: In siftDown, tracking the smallest among current, left, and right before swapping is critical. Swapping with the smaller child preserves the heap property: the smaller child moves up and its subtree remains valid. Swapping with the larger child would violate the heap property for that subtree. The loop termination (smallest === i) means no child is smaller than the current node — the heap property is locally satisfied.

common_mistakes: Sifting down by swapping with an arbitrary child instead of the smaller one — always swap with the smaller child (min-heap) or larger child (max-heap); swapping with the wrong child violates the heap property in the swapped subtree
Not checking i <= this.size before accessing left and right children in siftDown — accessing beyond the array bounds returns undefined, which compares incorrectly with numbers

Using O(n log n) repeated insert instead of O(n) heapify when building a heap from an existing array — heapify is strictly better for initialisation; always mention it when the interviewer asks 'how would you build a heap from an unsorted array?'
lessons.interview_relevance: Implement a heap from scratch appears at companies that want to test foundational CS depth. More commonly, interviewers ask 'explain how sift-up and sift-down work' and 'why is heapify O(n) instead of O(n log n)?'. The O(n) heapify proof — most nodes are near leaves where sift-down is cheap — is specifically tested at Google and Meta.

flashcards.front: Heap insert: two steps?
flashcards.back: 1) Append to end of array (maintains complete binary tree shape). 2) Sift-up: swap with parent while parent > current node (min-heap), restoring heap property.

flashcards.front: Heap extract-min: three steps?
flashcards.back: 1) Save root (the minimum). 2) Move last element to root position (pop from end). 3) Sift-down: swap with smaller child while current > either child. Return saved root.

flashcards.front: Sift-down: which child do you swap with?
flashcards.back: Always swap with the SMALLER child (min-heap). Swapping with the larger child would violate the heap property in that subtree.

flashcards.front: Why is sift-down O(log n)?
flashcards.back: At most one swap per level, and the heap has floor(log₂ n) levels. So at most log n swaps total.

flashcards.front: Heapify (build heap from array): complexity and approach?
flashcards.back: O(n) time. Apply sift-down to all non-leaf nodes from bottom (index n/2) to top (index 1). Bottom-up order ensures each sift-down operates on a valid heap below it.

flashcards.front: Why is heapify O(n) not O(n log n)?
flashcards.back: Most nodes are near leaves where sift-down is cheap. Half the nodes are leaves (0 swaps). Quarter need 1 swap. The sum across levels: Σ(k × n/2^(k+1)) for k=0..h converges to O(n).

flashcards.front: When to use heapify vs repeated insert?
flashcards.back: Heapify when building from an existing array: O(n). Repeated insert for n elements: O(n log n). Heapify is always better for batch construction.

practice_problems.title: Implement MinHeap from scratch with sift-up and sift-down

theory_mcq.question: Why does heap INSERT append to the END of the array before sifting UP, and heap EXTRACT replaces the root with the LAST element before sifting DOWN?
options: Both operations could start anywhere; the end/last choices are arbitrary

INSERT appends to the end to MAINTAIN THE COMPLETE BINARY TREE PROPERTY (always fill the next available left-to-right position), then sifts UP to restore the heap ordering; EXTRACT replaces the root with the last element for the SAME completeness reason (removing the last element from a complete tree keeps it complete), then sifts DOWN to restore ordering — in both cases, completeness is restored by working with the end/last position, then ordering is restored by sifting
Insert sifts down and extract sifts up — the question has them reversed
The choices are driven by cache performance, not heap correctness
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concepts: 'Insert: append to end (maintain completeness), sift-up to restore heap property' and 'Extract min: swap root with last element, remove last, sift-down root' — the completeness invariant (complete binary tree) and the heap ordering invariant are maintained separately, each step addressing one of them.

theory_mcq.question: Why does heapify (`fromArray`) run in O(n) time rather than O(n log n), even though it calls sift-down on roughly n/2 nodes?
options: heapify is O(n log n); the lesson's O(n) claim is incorrect

The O(n) proof relies on the observation that MOST nodes are NEAR THE LEAVES where sift-down costs very little: half the nodes are leaves (0 swaps), a quarter are at height 1 (at most 1 swap), an eighth at height 2 (at most 2 swaps), etc. — this geometric series sums to O(n) total swaps, much cheaper than the naive O(n log n) estimate that assumes every sift-down costs O(log n)
heapify is O(n) because it only calls sift-down on one node
heapify achieves O(n) by using a hash table to cache sift-down results
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Heapify O(n) proof: more nodes near leaves, sift-down costs less there' — the amortized analysis shows that the sum of all sift-down costs across the bottom-up pass is bounded by O(n) due to the geometric weight of nodes near the base of the tree, giving heapify a strictly better O(n) bound versus O(n log n) for n individual insertions.

logic_mcq.question: After inserting [5,3,8,1,4] into a MinHeap in order, what is the peek (minimum) and what does the first extractMin return, followed by the new peek?
options: peek=5, extractMin=5, new peek=3

peek=1, extractMin=1, new peek=3 — inserting 5,3,8,1,4 produces a valid min-heap with 1 at the root (since 1 is the minimum); extractMin correctly removes and returns 1 and the next minimum (3) becomes the new root — confirmed by direct execution
peek=1, extractMin=1, new peek=4
peek=3, extractMin=3, new peek=1
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: after inserting [5,3,8,1,4], sift-up operations ensure 1 (the minimum) reaches the root; extractMin returns 1 (swaps with last element, removes, sifts down), and 3 (the next smallest) becomes the new root as confirmed by the lesson's console.log outputs.

logic_mcq.question: In `_siftDown`, why is `smallest` initially set to `i` (the current node) rather than to the smallest child index directly?
options: smallest=i is a bug; it should always start at the left child

Starting `smallest = i` means: 'assume this node is already the smallest; check if any child is actually smaller'; if no child is smaller (both children are >= current), `smallest` remains `i`, the `if (smallest === i) break` fires, and the sift terminates correctly; this three-way comparison (current, left, right) in one pass determines whether to swap at all, and if so, which child to swap with
smallest must start at 0 to handle the empty heap case
smallest=i is used only for the root; other nodes start at their left child
logic_mcq.explanation: The `smallest = i` initialization sets the REFERENCE for comparison — it's progressively updated to the index of whichever of {i, left, right} holds the smallest value; if after checking both children `smallest` is still `i`, no child was smaller, the heap property is restored, and the loop terminates via the `break`.

syntax_mcq.question: In `extractMin()`, the special case `if (this.size === 1) return this.heap.pop()` is checked BEFORE the main extraction logic. Why is this case handled separately?
options: This case can be merged with the general case without affecting correctness

When only one element remains, `this.heap[1] = this.heap.pop()` would assign the popped value (the only element) back to index 1, leaving the heap with [null, value] instead of empty [null]; the special case avoids this: `this.heap.pop()` directly removes and returns the last (only) element, correctly producing an empty heap [null] afterward
The special case handles negative values incorrectly in the general case

lessons.title: Kth Largest Element
lessons.objective: Find the kth largest element in an array in O(n log k) using a fixed-size min-heap, and compare this with the O(n log n) sort approach and O(n) average quickselect approach.
concepts: Kth largest: maintain min-heap of size k
Invariant: heap always holds the k largest elements seen so far
Heap top (minimum of the heap) is the kth largest overall
O(n log k) time: n insertions each O(log k)
O(k) space: heap never exceeds size k
Why min-heap for kth largest: heap top is the smallest of the k largest
Quickselect: O(n) average, O(n²) worst case alternative
Sorting approach: O(n log n) simpler but worse
lessons.explanation: Finding the kth largest element with a min-heap of fixed size k: iterate through all n elements, inserting each into the min-heap. After inserting, if the heap size exceeds k, extract the minimum (removing the smallest element seen so far). After processing all n elements, the heap contains exactly the k largest elements, and the heap minimum (root) is the kth largest. The invariant: at every point, the heap holds the k largest elements seen so far. The minimum of those k elements (heap root) is by definition the kth largest. Time: O(n log k) because each insert and extract is O(log k) and we do at most 2n operations. Space: O(k) since the heap never exceeds size k+1. Compare with sorting: O(n log n) time O(1)-O(n) space, no streaming. Compare with quickselect: O(n) average O(n²) worst case O(1) space, not streaming-friendly. For streaming or when k << n, the min-heap approach is optimal.
lessons.analogy: Min-heap for kth largest is like a bouncer at an exclusive club that only allows the k tallest people inside. As each new person arrives, they enter the club. If the club is overfull (k+1 people), the shortest person is ejected. After everyone has tried to enter, the shortest person inside the club (the heap minimum) is the kth tallest person overall. The heap always holds the elite k, discarding anyone shorter than the current kth tallest.

code_example.explanation: For k=1 (find maximum), the min-heap approach is O(n log 1) = O(n) — same as a linear scan. For k=n (find minimum), it is O(n log n) — same as sorting. The sweet spot where min-heap beats sorting is when k << n. For k = sqrt(n), min-heap is O(n log sqrt(n)) = O(n * 0.5 * log n) = O(n log n / 2) which is better than full sort by a factor of 2.

common_mistakes: Using a max-heap instead of a min-heap for kth largest — a max-heap of size k would give you the k smallest elements with the largest at the top; for kth largest you need a min-heap so the heap root (minimum) is the kth largest
Not extracting the minimum after exceeding size k — without the size check and extract, the heap grows to size n and the heap minimum is the overall minimum, not the kth largest

Confusing kth largest with kth smallest — for kth smallest, use a max-heap of size k: keep the k smallest by ejecting the maximum whenever the heap exceeds k; the max-heap root is then the kth smallest

The expected answer demonstrates three solutions in increasing sophistication: sort O(n log n), min-heap O(n log k), quickselect O(n) average. Being able to explain when each is preferable (streaming vs in-memory, time vs space tradeoffs) is specifically asked at senior level.

lessons.title: Top K Frequent Elements
lessons.objective: Solve Top K Frequent Elements using three approaches — heap, bucket sort, and quickselect — selecting the optimal approach based on constraints.
concepts: Frequency map: O(n) build
Max-heap approach: extract k times O(n log n)
Min-heap of size k: O(n log k) — better when k << n
Bucket sort approach: O(n) using frequency as array index
Bucket sort advantage: O(n) beats O(n log k) for all k
Quickselect on frequency array: O(n) average
When O(n) bucket sort is not applicable: non-integer or unbounded frequencies
Heap stores (frequency, element) pairs for comparison
lessons.explanation: Top K Frequent Elements (Module 3 Lesson 7) is revisited here with the heap perspective. Three approaches: (1) Max-heap: insert all (frequency, element) pairs into a max-heap, then extract k times. O(n) to build frequency map, O(n) to build max-heap via heapify, O(k log n) to extract k times. Total O(n + k log n). (2) Min-heap of size k: iterate over all (frequency, element) pairs, maintain a min-heap by frequency. After processing all pairs, the heap contains the k most frequent elements. O(n log k). Better than approach 1 when k << n. (3) Bucket sort: since frequencies range from 1 to n, use frequency as an array index (Module 3 Lesson 7). O(n). The heap approach is more general and applies when frequencies are not bounded integers. For this specific problem, bucket sort is optimal. The lesson is: know all three approaches and select based on constraints.
lessons.analogy: Top K Frequent is like finding the k most-watched movies. The max-heap approach is like sorting all movies by watch count and picking the top k — O(n log n). The min-heap approach is like maintaining a VIP list of only k spots, replacing the least-watched VIP when a more popular movie comes along — O(n log k). The bucket sort approach is like having a board with columns numbered 1 to n (max possible watch count) and placing each movie in its column, then reading from the highest column downward — O(n).

code_example.explanation: For interviews, state all three approaches, explain their complexities, and recommend bucket sort as optimal for this specific problem. Then ask the interviewer: 'Are there constraints that rule out bucket sort?' (e.g. frequencies are floating-point, or elements are not hashable). If yes, fall back to the heap approach. This structured approach — state all solutions, select based on constraints — is exactly the engineering judgement interviewers evaluate.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to handle ties within a bucket in bucket sort — multiple elements can have the same frequency and land in the same bucket; collect them all before checking if you have reached k

Using the wrong heap type — a max-heap gives you the most frequent first but costs O(n log n) to build and extract; a min-heap of size k is O(n log k) but requires custom pair comparison with frequency as the priority key
Not mentioning bucket sort to the interviewer — providing only the heap solution without mentioning O(n) bucket sort misses the opportunity to demonstrate awareness of the optimal approach
lessons.interview_relevance: Top K Frequent Elements (#347) is Blind 75. This problem is one of the clearest tests of whether a candidate knows multiple approaches and can select the optimal one based on constraints. Interviewers specifically ask 'can you do better than O(n log k)?' to see if you know bucket sort. Knowing the answer separates strong candidates from average ones.

flashcards.front: Why can bucket sort be used here but not always?
flashcards.back: Because frequencies are integers bounded by [1, n]. Bucket sort requires bounded integer keys. For floating-point, unbounded, or non-integer keys, you cannot bucket-sort — use heap instead.

Downward iteration handles the edge case where all elements have the same frequency

The heap (or sort comparator) needs to ORDER elements by FREQUENCY — putting frequency as the first element of the pair makes it the natural comparison key when sorting `(a, b) => b[0] - a[0]`; if element value were first, the sorting would accidentally order by element value instead of frequency; the convention [frequency, element] makes the comparison key explicit and unambiguous
Putting frequency first is required by JavaScript's sort() function
Frequency must be first because it's always a larger number than the element value
logic_mcq.explanation: The pair's structure determines the comparison key: `[frequency, element]` with comparator `(a,b) => b[0]-a[0]` compares pairs by their FIRST element (frequency), ignoring the second; [element, frequency] with the same comparator would accidentally sort by element value, producing incorrect results.

`.fill([])` would place the SAME SINGLE array reference at every index — pushing to buckets[2] would also affect buckets[3], buckets[4], etc. (they all reference the same object); `.fill(null).map(() => [])` creates a NEW INDEPENDENT array for each index (the arrow function `() => []` is called once per element, creating fresh arrays), ensuring pushes to different buckets don't interfere
.fill([]) is correct but only for arrays shorter than 100 elements
.map(() => []) is required because .fill() doesn't work with arrays
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is a classic JavaScript reference-vs-value trap: `.fill([])` fills every slot with a reference to THE SAME array object — any mutation (push) to one bucket would appear in all buckets; `.fill(null).map(() => [])` creates n+1 DISTINCT array instances (the lambda creates a new `[]` for each map call), ensuring bucket independence.

lessons.title: K Closest Points To Origin
lessons.objective: Find the K closest points to the origin in O(n log k) using a max-heap of size k, and understand why Euclidean distance can be compared without the square root.
concepts: Euclidean distance: sqrt(x² + y²)
Distance comparison without sqrt: x² + y² is monotonically equivalent
Max-heap of size k: ejects the farthest point when size exceeds k
O(n log k) time: n insertions each O(log k)
Why max-heap for k closest: keep k closest by ejecting the farthest
Custom comparator: heap ordered by squared distance
Quickselect alternative: O(n) average
Result order: problem does not require sorted output
lessons.explanation: K Closest Points to Origin finds the k points with the smallest Euclidean distance from (0,0). Euclidean distance is sqrt(x² + y²), but since sqrt is a monotonically increasing function, comparing distances is equivalent to comparing squared distances. Using squared distances avoids the sqrt computation and keeps values as integers. The max-heap approach (analogous to kth largest but inverted): maintain a max-heap ordered by squared distance, keeping exactly k points. For each new point, compute its squared distance and insert into the heap. If the heap exceeds k, extract the maximum (farthest point, ejecting it). After all n points are processed, the heap contains the k closest points. The max-heap root is the farthest among the k closest — any new point closer than this root displaces it.
lessons.analogy: K closest points with a max-heap is like maintaining a VIP section at a concert where the k closest seats to the stage are always occupied by the closest fans. When a new fan arrives at a closer distance, the fan sitting furthest among the VIP k is ejected to make room. The max-heap always knows who the most distant VIP is, enabling O(log k) ejection.

code_example.explanation: Using squared distances (x² + y²) instead of actual distances (sqrt(x² + y²)) is valid because sqrt is monotonically increasing: if A² < B² then sqrt(A²) < sqrt(B²). This optimisation avoids floating-point arithmetic and square root computation, keeping all comparisons in integer space. Always mention this to the interviewer — it signals awareness of computational efficiency beyond algorithmic complexity.

common_mistakes: Using a min-heap instead of max-heap for k closest — a min-heap of all points gives the closest at the top but requires storing all n points; a max-heap of size k efficiently maintains only the k closest by ejecting the farthest
Computing actual Euclidean distance with Math.sqrt instead of squared distance — sqrt is unnecessary for comparisons and introduces floating-point imprecision
Not noting that the output does not need to be sorted — the problem asks for any k closest points; the heap gives them in unsorted order, which is acceptable and avoids an extra O(k log k) sort
lessons.interview_relevance: K Closest Points to Origin (#973) is Blind 75. It is used to test: (1) heap intuition (max-heap for closest, min-heap for largest), (2) distance optimisation (squared vs actual), (3) awareness of quickselect as an O(n) alternative. Mentioning all three approaches and selecting based on constraints — streaming or not, in-memory or not — demonstrates senior-level thinking.

options: Squared distance produces different ordering than actual distance for some inputs

Since sqrt() is a MONOTONICALLY INCREASING function, comparing x₁²+y₁² < x₂²+y₂² produces the SAME relative ordering as comparing √(x₁²+y₁²) < √(x₂²+y₂²) — the square root never changes which distance is larger or smaller; using squared distance avoids the computationally more expensive Math.sqrt() call for every comparison, since square root evaluation involves an iterative approximation internally
Squared distance only works correctly when all coordinates are positive integers
sqrt() would cause floating-point rounding that makes comparisons unreliable
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Distance comparison without sqrt: x²+y² is monotonically equivalent' — sqrt() preserves ordering because it's strictly increasing; since all distance comparisons only need to determine relative order (not absolute values), squared distance gives identical comparison results while avoiding the sqrt computation.

theory_mcq.question: For K closest points, we use a MAX-heap (not a min-heap). Why is a MAX-heap the right choice here?
options: The heap type is identical for k-closest and k-largest problems

We need to efficiently EJECT the FARTHEST point whenever a closer one arrives — a max-heap of size k keeps the farthest-of-the-k-closest at the ROOT, where it can be compared and ejected in O(log k); if we used a min-heap, the farthest point would be buried deep in the heap with no O(1) access, making ejection O(n)
A max-heap is used because distance values are always positive
A max-heap is needed only when coordinates include negative values
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Why max-heap for k closest: keep k closest by ejecting the farthest' and 'Heap root = farthest among the k closest (to eject when oversized)' — the max-heap invariant puts the LARGEST (farthest) element at the root, giving O(1) access to the candidate for ejection when the heap exceeds size k.

[1,3] has squared distance 1+3=4; [-2,2] has squared distance 2+2=4; both are equidistant
The function returns [[1,3]] because 1+3<(-2)+2
Both points are returned regardless of k

options: [3,3]: 18, [5,-1]: 26, [-2,4]: 20; the 2 closest are [3,3] (dist=18) and [-2,4] (dist=20) — these are the correct k=2 closest regardless of output order
All three points have equal distance; any 2 can be returned

syntax_mcq.question: In `const sqDist = ([x, y]) => x * x + y * y`, what does `([x, y])` in the parameter position accomplish?
options: It calls the point's constructor with two arguments

This is ARRAY DESTRUCTURING in the function parameter: when `sqDist` receives a point array like `[3,3]`, JavaScript automatically unpacks the array and binds the first element to `x` and the second to `y` — allowing direct use of `x` and `y` in the function body without an explicit `const [x,y] = point` declaration inside
([x,y]) creates a new array from the point's coordinates
This syntax only works when the point array contains exactly two elements
syntax_mcq.explanation: Destructuring in function parameters is a concise JavaScript pattern: `([x, y]) => ...` is equivalent to `(point) => { const [x, y] = point; return ...; }` — it immediately unpacks the array argument into named variables `x` and `y`, making the body of the arrow function cleaner and more readable.

lessons.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
lessons.objective: Merge K sorted linked lists in O(N log k) using a min-heap that always holds the current smallest unprocessed head, and understand why this beats the naive O(Nk) approach.
concepts: Naive merge: repeatedly find minimum across k heads O(Nk)
Min-heap approach: O(log k) per extraction
Heap stores (value, list_head) pairs
After extracting min: push next node of that list
O(N log k) total: N nodes extracted, each O(log k)
Dummy head for clean output list construction
Connection to Module 6 divide-and-conquer approach O(N log k)
Both approaches have same asymptotic complexity
lessons.explanation: Merge K Sorted Lists has N total nodes across k lists. Naive approach: find the minimum among k heads by scanning all k, append it to the result, advance that list's pointer. O(k) per node times N nodes = O(Nk). Min-heap approach: initialise the heap with the head node of each list (k nodes initially). Extract the minimum (O(log k)), append it to the result, then push the next node of that list into the heap (O(log k)). Repeat until the heap is empty. Each of the N total nodes is inserted into and extracted from the heap exactly once: O(N log k) total. The heap always holds exactly one node from each non-exhausted list, maintaining O(k) size. This is a classic application of the heap as a 'multi-way merge' structure — it efficiently tracks the current minimum across multiple sorted sequences simultaneously.
lessons.analogy: Merge k sorted lists with a heap is like a tournament where k athletes run simultaneously and you always record the current leader. Instead of watching all k athletes at once (naive O(k) per step), you have a scoreboard (heap) that always shows who is in the lead. When the leader finishes a segment, you update the scoreboard with their new position. The scoreboard update is O(log k) regardless of how many athletes there are.

code_example.explanation: The list_index in each heap entry [value, idx, node] is a tiebreaker when two nodes have equal values. Without it, heap comparisons between arrays of length 2 would compare the node objects, which is not defined. Always include a stable tiebreaker (index, insertion order, or any secondary key) when heap entries might have equal primary keys.

common_mistakes: Not pushing the next node after extracting the minimum — after using a node, its successor must be added to the heap to continue processing that list; forgetting this produces a truncated merged list
Initialising the heap with all N nodes upfront instead of only k heads — this wastes O(N) space and O(N log N) initial heapify time; only add k head nodes initially
Not handling empty lists in the initial setup — some lists may be null; always check if lists[i] is non-null before inserting into the heap

The NAIVE approach scans all k current list heads to find the minimum at each step — O(k) per extraction × N total extractions = O(Nk); the HEAP approach maintains a heap of size k (one current head per list), making each extraction and re-insertion O(log k) instead of O(k) — the heap's structure lets us find and replace the minimum in O(log k) rather than O(k)

theory_mcq.question: In the heap-based merge, after extracting the minimum node, why is the NEXT NODE from the SAME LIST pushed back into the heap?
options: The next node is pushed only when the current list is exhausted

The heap maintains the invariant of ONE representative (current head) from EACH non-exhausted list — after the current minimum is output, its list still has remaining elements that must be considered; pushing the next node from that same list restores the one-representative-per-list invariant, ensuring the heap always contains candidates from every list that still has elements to contribute
All nodes from all lists are pushed at the start; no insertions happen during merge
The next node is pushed to prevent the heap from becoming empty
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core of the k-way merge pattern: the heap always holds exactly one 'representative' from each non-exhausted list; replacing the extracted minimum with the next node from the same list maintains this invariant, ensuring every remaining element from every list remains reachable through the heap's representatives.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson notes that heap-based mergeKLists and divide-and-conquer mergeKLists (from Module 6) both achieve O(N log k). What is fundamentally different between the two approaches despite having the same asymptotic complexity?
options: They are identical implementations with different function names

Heap-based: processes nodes GREEDILY one-at-a-time using a priority queue, always picking the current global minimum across all k lists; divide-and-conquer: recursively PAIRS UP lists and merges them in rounds (like merge sort on lists), never maintaining a heap but instead fully merging pairs; same O(N log k) complexity from different constants — heap may have better cache performance in practice, divide-and-conquer may have simpler implementation
Heap-based is O(N log k) while divide-and-conquer is O(N log N)
The two approaches have different space complexities: heap is O(N), divide-and-conquer is O(1)
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson: 'Connection to Module 6 divide-and-conquer approach O(N log k). Both approaches have same asymptotic complexity' — the key difference is the mechanism: heap works element-by-element from the current global minimum, while divide-and-conquer works list-by-list in batches; both achieve O(N log k) via different structural arguments.

list_index is needed to access the original lists array for pushing next nodes
syntax_mcq.explanation: While `node.next` gives the next node directly (making list_index technically redundant for node traversal), including list_index is a common practical choice for clarity and tie-breaking — when node values are equal, the list_index provides a stable secondary comparison key, and it explicitly documents which source list each entry belongs to.

lessons.title: Task Scheduler
lessons.objective: Solve Task Scheduler using a max-heap combined with a cooldown queue to simulate CPU task scheduling, and derive the minimum idle time formula.
concepts: Task Scheduler problem: CPU cooldown n between same task types
Max-heap by frequency: always execute the most frequent available task
Cooldown queue: tasks cooling down stored with their re-available time
Time simulation: advance clock, check cooldown expirations
Mathematical formula: time = max(len(tasks), (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countMaxFreq)
Formula derivation: optimal grouping of most frequent task
Both approaches: simulation O(t * log u) vs formula O(26 log 26) = O(1)
Greedy insight: always executing the most frequent available task is optimal
lessons.explanation: Task Scheduler gives a list of tasks (A-Z) and a cooldown period n: the same task type cannot be executed within n time units of itself. Find the minimum time to complete all tasks. Greedy simulation approach: use a max-heap by frequency to always execute the most frequent available task. Use a cooldown queue of (frequency_remaining, available_at_time) pairs. At each time step: pop available tasks from the cooldown queue back into the heap. If the heap is non-empty, execute the top task (decrement frequency) and push it to the cooldown queue with available_at = current_time + n + 1. If the heap is empty but the queue is non-empty, the CPU is idle — advance time to the next available task. Total time is counted. Mathematical formula: the minimum time is max(total_tasks, (max_frequency - 1) * (n + 1) + count_of_max_frequency_tasks). This formula comes from the observation that the most frequent task determines the frame structure.
lessons.analogy: Task Scheduler is like a chef managing multiple types of dishes where the same dish must rest n minutes between preparations. The greedy strategy is always preparing the dish with the most remaining servings when available. The cooldown queue is the resting timer for each dish type. The formula gives the theoretical minimum time based on how many servings of the most popular dish need to be made.

code_example.explanation: The formula max(tasks.length, (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countMaxFreq) has two cases. If the formula exceeds tasks.length, idle time is needed and the formula gives the answer. If tasks.length exceeds the formula, there are enough diverse tasks to keep the CPU busy without idle time, and tasks.length is the answer. The Math.max handles both cases in one line.

common_mistakes: Using only the formula without understanding the greedy simulation — the formula is elegant but the simulation demonstrates the actual greedy strategy; interviewers often ask you to explain the simulation first
Forgetting that the formula result can be less than tasks.length — when there are many diverse tasks, no idle time is needed; taking Math.max with tasks.length is required
Not counting how many tasks share the maximum frequency in the formula — if A and B both have frequency 3 (the maximum), countMaxFreq is 2, not 1; this affects the last cycle length
lessons.interview_relevance: Task Scheduler (#621) is Blind 75. It has two valid approaches — simulation and formula — and interviewers expect both. The greedy simulation with a heap demonstrates algorithmic thinking; the formula demonstrates mathematical insight. Companies typically want both: 'implement it, then derive the closed-form formula.'
lessons.mini_challenge: Verify the formula gives 8 for (['A','A','A','B','B','B'], n=2) and 9 for (['A','A','A','B','B','B','C','C','C'], n=2). Then implement the simulation and verify it gives the same results. Finally, construct an example where the formula gives a smaller value than tasks.length and verify Math.max returns tasks.length. Explain the geometric structure of the 'frames' that the formula is based on.

flashcards.front: Task Scheduler greedy rule?
flashcards.back: Always execute the most frequent available task. This minimises idle time by using cool-down periods for less frequent tasks.

flashcards.front: Task Scheduler: what two data structures are used?
flashcards.back: 1) Max-heap by remaining frequency — always access the most frequent task. 2) Cooldown queue — stores (remaining_freq, re_available_time) for tasks currently cooling down.

flashcards.front: Task Scheduler formula?
flashcards.back: max(len(tasks), (maxFreq - 1) × (n + 1) + countMaxFreq). Where maxFreq = highest task frequency, countMaxFreq = number of task types with that frequency.

flashcards.front: Why Math.max(tasks.length, formula) in Task Scheduler?
flashcards.back: If enough diverse tasks exist to fill every slot without idling, tasks.length is the answer. The formula gives the minimum time if the most-frequent task forces idle periods — but idle periods only occur when tasks.length < formula.

flashcards.front: What is a 'frame' in Task Scheduler formula?
flashcards.back: A frame is a group of (n+1) time slots: one slot for the most-frequent task + n slots for cooldown. There are (maxFreq-1) complete frames, plus a final partial frame of countMaxFreq slots.

flashcards.front: countMaxFreq in the formula: what is it?
flashcards.back: The number of distinct task types that share the maximum frequency. If A and B both appear 3 times (the max), countMaxFreq = 2. They fill the last partial frame side by side.

quiz.question: Tasks=['A','A','A','B','B','B'], n=2. Formula result?
quiz.explanation: (maxFreq-1)×(n+1)+countMaxFreq = (3-1)×(2+1)+2 = 2×3+2 = 8. tasks.length=6. max(6,8)=8.

quiz.question: Tasks=['A','A','A','B','B','B','C','C','C'], n=2. Formula result?
quiz.explanation: (3-1)×(2+1)+3=2×3+3=9. tasks.length=9. max(9,9)=9. Frame: ABC ABC ABC — no idle slots needed.

quiz.question: When does the formula give a smaller value than tasks.length?
options: When n=0 (no cooldown required)
When there are many diverse tasks that fill all cooldown slots without idling
When all tasks are the same type
When k=1
quiz.explanation: When tasks are diverse enough to fill every time slot: A B C A B C... no idle needed. tasks.length captures this. Math.max picks tasks.length over the formula.

quiz.question: Why use a max-heap (not min-heap) for Task Scheduler simulation?
options: Max-heap gives sorted output
Greedy: always execute the MOST frequent available task to minimise future idle time
Min-heap can't store frequencies
Max-heap uses less memory
quiz.explanation: The greedy strategy is to always run the most frequent available task. Max-heap gives O(log k) access to the highest-frequency task (k ≤ 26 for A-Z).

theory_mcq.question: What is the mathematical formula for Task Scheduler, and what does each term represent?
options: result = tasks.length + n (just add the cooldown to total tasks)

result = max(tasks.length, (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countMaxFreq) where: maxFreq is the frequency of the most-common task; (maxFreq-1) is the number of COMPLETE scheduling cycles before the last; (n+1) is the length of each cycle (1 execution slot + n cooldown slots); countMaxFreq is the number of tasks tied for highest frequency (filling the tail of the last partial cycle); tasks.length is the floor — if tasks fill every slot without idling, no extra time is needed
result = maxFreq * (n+1) (simple multiplication of cycles and cycle length)
result = (maxFreq-1) * n + tasks.length (based on idle time only)
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's formula and example: 'AAABBB n=2: (3-1)*(2+1) + 2 = 8' — 2 complete cycles of length 3 (A_B or AB_) plus a final 2-slot partial cycle (AB); the max with tasks.length handles the case where tasks are dense enough that no idle time is needed at all.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the greedy insight 'always execute the most frequent available task' lead to the optimal (minimum time) schedule?
options: This greedy choice is not optimal; dynamic programming is always required

The most-frequent task is the BOTTLENECK that forces the most idle time if not addressed proactively — by always executing the most frequent available task first, we minimize the WAITING TIME for the most-constrained task type; any strategy that delays the most frequent task would increase the total schedule length because the bottleneck task's cooldowns would create more unavoidable idle periods
The greedy choice only works when n=0 (no cooldown)
Executing least-frequent tasks first would be equally optimal
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core greedy argument: the task with maximum frequency determines the MINIMUM number of required scheduling frames; always processing the most frequent available task ensures this bottleneck task gets scheduled as early as possible in each cooldown window, minimizing idle time across all frames.

logic_mcq.question: For `leastIntervalFormula(['A','A','A','B','B','B'], n=2)`, trace the formula computation and verify the result is 8.
options: maxFreq=3, countMaxFreq=2, formula=(3-1)*(2+1)+2=8, tasks.length=6, max(6,8)=8 ✓ — verified by direct execution
maxFreq=6, formula=6*(2+1)=18
result=6 because tasks.length=6 is sufficient with no idle
result=12 because each task needs n=2 cooldown slots
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact computation: maxFreq=3 (both A and B appear 3 times), countMaxFreq=2 (two tasks at maximum frequency), formula = (3-1)*(2+1) + 2 = 2*3 + 2 = 8; tasks.length=6; max(6,8)=8; the optimal schedule A B _ A B _ A B uses exactly 8 time units with 2 idle slots — confirmed by direct execution.

logic_mcq.question: For `leastIntervalFormula(['A','A','A','B','B','B','C','C','C'], n=2)`, why does `tasks.length=9` take precedence over the formula result of 8?
options: tasks.length never takes precedence; the formula always gives the correct answer

When there are enough distinct task types to fill every slot without any idle time, the minimum schedule length equals just tasks.length (no idle slots needed) — here, 3 task types × 3 occurrences each = 9 tasks fit perfectly into A B C A B C A B C with n=2 cooldown satisfied (A never repeats within 2 slots); the formula gives 8 which is too short (it only accounts for A and B's frequency, missing C), so max(9,8)=9 correctly captures this
The formula is wrong for cases with 3 or more task types
tasks.length=9 takes precedence because 9>8 in absolute value
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by the lesson's example: '9 tasks: A B C A B C A B C (9 time units, 0 idle). Formula: (3-1)*(2+1)+3=8. Math.max(9,8)=9 ✓' — the formula models the MINIMUM based on the most frequent task's structure; when many task types exist, they fill all available slots and the actual number of tasks becomes the binding constraint.

syntax_mcq.question: In `leastIntervalFormula`, `freq[t.charCodeAt(0) - 65]++` increments the frequency for task `t`. Why is `charCodeAt(0) - 65` the correct array index for uppercase task names?
options: 65 is subtracted because JavaScript arrays are 1-indexed

Uppercase letters 'A' through 'Z' have ASCII/Unicode code points 65 through 90; subtracting 65 maps 'A'→0, 'B'→1, ..., 'Z'→25 — perfectly indexing the 26-element freq array; this converts a character to its 0-based alphabet position, which is the standard approach for fixed-alphabet character frequency counting
charCodeAt(0) - 65 only works for characters after the letter 'A'
65 must be subtracted to prevent the index from exceeding 26
syntax_mcq.explanation: Standard alphabet indexing: ASCII 'A'=65, 'B'=66, ..., 'Z'=90; subtracting the baseline (65, ASCII of 'A') gives 0-indexed positions 0-25 for the 26 uppercase letters, directly usable as indices into the 26-slot freq array — this pattern appears throughout competitive programming for lowercase ('a'=97, subtract 97) and uppercase ('A'=65, subtract 65) alphabet problems.

lessons.title: Find Median From Data Stream
lessons.objective: Design a data structure that supports adding numbers one at a time and returning the median in O(log n) per insertion and O(1) per median query, using two heaps.
concepts: Median definition: middle value (odd n) or average of two middles (even n)
Two-heap invariant: max-heap (lower half) and min-heap (upper half)
Size invariant: maxHeap.size ≥ minHeap.size and maxHeap.size - minHeap.size ≤ 1
Balance step: re-balance after each insertion
O(log n) insert: heap push plus one or two re-balances
O(1) findMedian: maxHeap top (odd n) or average of both tops (even n)
Why two heaps: each half maintains its extreme in O(1)
Space: O(n) total
lessons.explanation: Find Median from Data Stream requires: addNum in O(log n) and findMedian in O(1). The naive approach stores all values and sorts; O(n log n) per median. The two-heap approach: maintain a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half. Invariant: (1) every element in the max-heap is ≤ every element in the min-heap, and (2) the max-heap has at most one more element than the min-heap. With this invariant, the median is: if sizes are equal, average of max-heap top and min-heap top; if max-heap is larger, max-heap top. Insert procedure: if the new value is ≤ max-heap top, push to max-heap, else push to min-heap. Then re-balance: if max-heap size exceeds min-heap size by more than 1, move max-heap top to min-heap; if min-heap size exceeds max-heap size, move min-heap top to max-heap. Each insertion requires O(log n) for the push and at most one re-balance of O(log n).
lessons.analogy: Two heaps for median is like a theatre with two halves: left half and right half. The left half is organised so the person in the back-right corner (max-heap top) is the tallest on that side. The right half is organised so the front-left person (min-heap top) is the shortest on that side. The median person sits between these two. When a new audience member arrives, they go to whichever half they belong in based on their height. If one side gets one extra person, one person crosses the aisle to re-balance.

code_example.explanation: The simplified array version verifies correctness at O(n) per insert. The two-heap version achieves O(log n) per insert. In interviews, implement the two-heap version and use the array version to verify your test cases. The key invariant to state clearly: 'max-heap holds the lower half, min-heap holds the upper half, and max-heap is allowed to have at most one more element than min-heap.'

common_mistakes: Using two max-heaps or two min-heaps instead of one of each — the lower half needs a max-heap (to access its maximum in O(1)) and the upper half needs a min-heap (to access its minimum in O(1)); using the same type for both gives O(n) median access
Not rebalancing after insertion — without rebalancing, the two heaps can have arbitrarily different sizes and the median formula breaks down
Off-by-one in the rebalance condition — the invariant allows maxHeap.size = minHeap.size (even total) or maxHeap.size = minHeap.size + 1 (odd total); any other size difference requires rebalancing
lessons.interview_relevance: Find Median from Data Stream (#295) is Blind 75 and one of the hardest Blind 75 problems. It appears at senior interview rounds at every major company. The two-heap insight — use a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half so that both halves' extremes are accessible in O(1) — is a creative data structure design that interviewers use to distinguish candidates. Not knowing this is acceptable; deriving it from first principles during the interview is exceptional.

flashcards.front: Find Median from Data Stream: two-heap invariant?
flashcards.back: maxHeap (lower half) size ≥ minHeap (upper half) size. AND maxHeap size - minHeap size ≤ 1. Ensures maxHeap has the median element or both halves split it evenly.

flashcards.front: Find Median: which heap holds which half?
flashcards.back: maxHeap = lower half (root = largest of smaller values). minHeap = upper half (root = smallest of larger values). Every element in maxHeap ≤ every element in minHeap.

flashcards.front: Find Median: how to read the median?
flashcards.back: If maxHeap.size > minHeap.size: median = maxHeap.peek(). If equal sizes: median = (maxHeap.peek() + minHeap.peek()) / 2.

flashcards.front: Find Median insertion steps?
flashcards.back: 1) Insert into correct heap: if val ≤ maxHeap.peek(), push to maxHeap; else push to minHeap. 2) Rebalance: if maxHeap is 2+ larger than minHeap, move maxHeap top to minHeap. If minHeap is larger than maxHeap, move minHeap top to maxHeap.

flashcards.front: Why O(1) for findMedian?
flashcards.back: Median is always at the top of one or both heaps. peek() is O(1). No searching needed.

flashcards.front: Why two heaps and not one sorted array?
flashcards.back: Sorted array: O(n) insert (binary shift), O(1) median. Two heaps: O(log n) insert, O(1) median. Heaps win on insert — critical for streaming with many additions.

quiz.explanation: maxHeap.size=2 > minHeap.size=1 → odd total → median = maxHeap.peek() = 2.

quiz.question: addNum(5) to MedianFinder where maxHeap=[2,1], minHeap=[3]. Where does 5 go initially?
options: maxHeap — it goes in lower half
minHeap — 5 > maxHeap.peek()=2 so it goes in upper half
Either heap — rebalancing fixes it
A new third heap
quiz.explanation: 5 > maxHeap.peek()=2 → goes to minHeap. minHeap=[3,5]. Rebalance: minHeap.size(2) > maxHeap.size(2)? No (both 2 after insert). Actually minHeap becomes size 2, maxHeap size 2 → balanced. Wait: after insert: maxH=[2,1](size 2), minH=[3,5](size 2). Balanced → no rebalance needed.

quiz.question: Why can't you use two min-heaps (instead of one max and one min)?
options: Two min-heaps use more memory
Lower half needs max-heap so its maximum (the potential median) is accessible in O(1)
Two min-heaps would give wrong results for even n
Min-heaps don't support the rebalance operation
quiz.explanation: The lower half's MAXIMUM is the left-middle element (potential median). With a min-heap for the lower half, finding its maximum requires O(n) search. Max-heap gives O(1) access to exactly what we need.

quiz.question: MedianFinder insert time complexity?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: One heap push O(log n) plus at most one rebalance (one push + one pop, both O(log n)). Total: O(log n) per insertion.

theory_mcq.question: What is the TWO-HEAP invariant maintained by MedianFinder, and why does this invariant allow O(1) median retrieval?
options: Both heaps have exactly the same size at all times

The two-heap invariant has two parts: (1) PARTITION: every element in maxHeap (lower half) is <= every element in minHeap (upper half); (2) SIZE BALANCE: maxHeap.size >= minHeap.size AND maxHeap.size - minHeap.size <= 1; this enables O(1) median retrieval because: if sizes are unequal, the median is maxHeap.peek() (the top of the larger heap = middle element); if sizes are equal, the median is (maxHeap.peek() + minHeap.peek()) / 2 (average of two middle elements)
Each heap holds exactly half the elements; the median is always the average of both tops
maxHeap always holds exactly n/2 elements; minHeap holds the rest
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact invariants: 'Size invariant: maxHeap.size ≥ minHeap.size and maxHeap.size - minHeap.size ≤ 1' and 'O(1) findMedian: maxHeap top (odd n) or average of both tops (even n)' — the invariants together guarantee the middle element is always at maxHeap's top when n is odd, or split between both tops when n is even.

theory_mcq.question: In the MedianFinder rebalancing step, when does an element move from maxHeap to minHeap vs from minHeap to maxHeap?
options: Elements always move from maxHeap to minHeap during rebalancing

From maxHeap to minHeap: when maxHeap has 2+ more elements than minHeap (maxHeap grew too large — move the max of maxHeap to minHeap to restore balance); from minHeap to maxHeap: when minHeap is LARGER than maxHeap (violating the maxHeap-at-least-as-large rule — move the min of minHeap to maxHeap); in both cases the element moved is the extreme of the oversized heap, which maintains the partition invariant
Rebalancing always moves the most recently inserted element
Elements are never moved between heaps; insertion decides the final heap
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact rebalancing code: 'if maxHeap.size > minHeap.size + 1: move extractMax to minHeap' (maxHeap too large) and 'else if minHeap.size > maxHeap.size: move extractMin to maxHeap' (minHeap became larger) — always moving the extreme of the overfull heap preserves the partition invariant.

0 means insert at position 0 (the beginning of the array)
0 is the value to insert when num is undefined
splice's second argument is always 0 for sorted arrays

lessons.title: Design Twitter Feed
lessons.objective: Design a simplified Twitter feed that returns the 10 most recent tweets from a user and their followees using a heap-based merge of multiple sorted tweet streams.
concepts: Twitter feed: merge k per-user tweet lists to get top 10 most recent
Tweet ordering by timestamp: global counter ensures total ordering
Per-user tweet storage: deque/array of (timestamp, tweetId) pairs
Max-heap to merge: extract 10 most recent across all followees
O(F * T + 10 log F) getNewsFeed: F=followees, T=tweets per user
Follow and unfollow: Set per user, O(1) add/remove
Connection to Merge K Sorted Lists: same pattern applied to tweet streams
Data model: userId -> {tweets, following}
lessons.explanation: Design Twitter (LeetCode #355) requires: postTweet, getNewsFeed (top 10 most recent tweets from self and followees), follow, and unfollow. The heap-based solution: each user maintains a list of their tweets in reverse-chronological order (most recent first), with a global timestamp to ensure total ordering across users. getNewsFeed initialises a max-heap with the most recent tweet of each followee (and self). Extract 10 times: each extraction pops the max-timestamp tweet and pushes the next tweet from that user's list. This is exactly Merge K Sorted Lists applied to tweet streams. Time for getNewsFeed: O(F) to initialise the heap with the first tweet from each of F followees, then O(10 log F) for 10 extractions. Total O(F + 10 log F) = O(F log F).
lessons.analogy: Design Twitter's getNewsFeed is like a news aggregator reading the most recent headline from each of F newspapers you subscribe to. Instead of reading all F newspapers cover-to-cover (O(F*T)), you create a heap of 'current front page' for each paper. Each time you extract the latest headline, you flip to the next page of that paper and add it to the heap. After 10 extractions, you have the 10 most recent headlines across all papers.

code_example.explanation: The global timestamp counter (incremented on every postTweet) ensures total ordering across all users. Tweets from different users posted at the same time (in the same test case) are distinguished by their timestamp values. The tweetIndex in the heap entry tracks which tweet from a user's list was last extracted, enabling O(1) access to the next tweet from that user.

common_mistakes: Not including the user themselves in getNewsFeed — a user should see their own tweets as well as their followees' tweets; the users set must include userId
Not handling the case where a user has no tweets or no followees — both conditions must be checked before accessing tweets or following sets

Using a global sorted list instead of per-user tweet lists — a global list makes unfollow O(n) to rebuild the feed; per-user lists with a heap merge gives O(F log F) for getNewsFeed and O(1) for follow/unfollow

The heap-based merge is the algorithmic insight; the data model (per-user tweet arrays, followee sets, global timestamp) is the design insight. Being able to justify every design decision — why per-user arrays, why a Set for following, why a global counter — is what interviewers evaluate.

theory_mcq.question: How does the Twitter feed design use the same k-way merge pattern from Lesson 6 (Merge K Sorted Lists)?
options: The Twitter feed doesn't use k-way merge; it uses a completely different approach

Each user's tweet list is a SORTED STREAM (sorted descending by timestamp/recency); getNewsFeed must return the 10 most recent tweets across all followees — this is exactly k-way merge where k=number of followees: initialize a max-heap with each user's most recent tweet, extract the maximum timestamp tweet, push the next tweet from that user's list; repeat until 10 tweets are collected — O(F*T + 10 log F) where F=followees, T=tweets per user
k-way merge is only used in sorted lists; tweets aren't sorted
The feed uses k-way merge but only when k > 10 followees
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit connection: 'Connection to Merge K Sorted Lists: same pattern applied to tweet streams' — per-user tweet arrays sorted by descending timestamp are the 'sorted lists'; a max-heap ordered by timestamp does the k-way merge, extracting the most recent tweet at each step and replacing it with the next from the same user's stream.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the Twitter class use a GLOBAL TIMESTAMP COUNTER rather than real wall-clock timestamps?
options: Wall-clock timestamps are more efficient than a counter

A global monotonically-increasing counter guarantees TOTAL ORDERING of all tweets — two tweets can never have the same counter value (unlike real timestamps which could collide at millisecond resolution), and the counter grows strictly with insertion order; this ensures the max-heap comparison `b[0]-a[0]` always produces a deterministic ordering, making the getNewsFeed output predictable and reproducible regardless of timing
The counter is used only as a debugging tool
Wall-clock timestamps would require network synchronization across users
theory_mcq.explanation: A global counter provides a STRICT total order (no two tweets share a timestamp) that's simpler and more reliable than real wall-clock time for algorithmic purposes — the counter increments on every postTweet call, ensuring a clear before/after relationship between any two tweets, which the max-heap needs for correct ordering.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the Twitter test sequence: postTweet(1,5), follow(1,2), postTweet(2,6), getNewsFeed(1). What does getNewsFeed return, and why is tweet 6 returned before tweet 5?
options: getNewsFeed returns [5,6] because user 1's tweets come before followees

getNewsFeed returns [6,5] — tweet 5 has timestamp 0 (first tweet posted), tweet 6 has timestamp 1 (posted later); the max-heap orders by timestamp descending, so timestamp=1 (tweet 6) is extracted first; user 1's tweet 5 (timestamp=0) is extracted second; result=[6,5] confirming 'more recent tweets appear first' — confirmed by direct execution
getNewsFeed returns [6] only because user 2 is being followed
getNewsFeed returns [5,6] because tweets are ordered by userId
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: tweet 5 gets timestamp 0 (postTweet called first), tweet 6 gets timestamp 1 (called second); the max-heap extracts by highest timestamp first → tweet 6 (ts=1) before tweet 5 (ts=0) → [6,5]; after unfollow(1,2), getNewsFeed(1) returns only [5].

logic_mcq.question: In `getNewsFeed`, `this.tweets.get(userId).unshift([this.timestamp++, tweetId])` uses `unshift` rather than `push`. Why does this produce more efficient getNewsFeed performance?
options: unshift and push are equivalent; the choice is arbitrary

Using `unshift` (prepend) keeps each user's tweet array sorted with the MOST RECENT tweet at index 0 — when getNewsFeed initializes the heap, it always accesses `userTweets[0]` (index 0) to get the user's most recent tweet as the starting heap entry; if push (append) were used, the most recent tweet would be at the last index, requiring idx=userTweets.length-1 initialization and backward traversal through the tweet stream
unshift is faster than push for large arrays
unshift is required because Twitter only stores the 10 most recent tweets per user
logic_mcq.explanation: The heap-based k-way merge starts from each user's MOST RECENT tweet (index 0) and progresses to older tweets (index 1, 2, ...) — by prepending with unshift, the most recent tweet is always at index 0, perfectly aligned with the heap's initialization pattern; this makes both initialization and the 'next tweet from same user' step straightforward (idx+1).

syntax_mcq.question: In `getNewsFeed`, `const users = new Set([userId])` initializes a Set with the user's own ID, then adds followees. Why use a Set rather than an Array?
options: Arrays cannot contain user IDs; only Sets can

A Set AUTOMATICALLY DEDUPLICATES — if userId follows themselves (or a followee's ID equals userId), the Set ensures they appear only ONCE in the iteration, preventing duplicate tweet processing; also, Set provides O(1) membership testing which, while not used here directly, is a natural fit for deduplicating user IDs across the followee list
Set iteration is faster than Array iteration for small collections
The Set is required because users.add() is only available on Sets
syntax_mcq.explanation: The Set deduplication property prevents double-counting: if a user follows themselves (a valid edge case), using an Array would include userId twice and process their tweets twice; a Set ensures each userId appears at most once, producing correct feed results without explicit duplicate checking.

lessons.title: Heap Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Recognise the three heap application patterns — top-K, k-way merge, and running statistics — within 60 seconds of reading any heap problem.
concepts: Pattern 1: Top-K using fixed-size heap O(n log k)
Pattern 2: K-way merge using heap of k heads O(N log k)
Pattern 3: Running statistics using two heaps or sliding window heap
Heap type selection: min-heap for k largest, max-heap for k smallest
When heap beats sorting: k << n, streaming, repeated queries
When sorting beats heap: small n, need sorted output, one-time query
Module 9 Blind 75 problems mapped
Skills unlocked: Heap, Priority Queue, Greedy with Heap
lessons.explanation: All heap problems in this module map to three patterns. Pattern 1 — Top-K: maintain a fixed-size heap of k elements. Use a min-heap to find the k largest (eject smallest when overfull). Use a max-heap to find the k smallest (eject largest when overfull). Problems: Kth Largest, K Closest, Top K Frequent, K Pairs with Smallest Sums. Pattern 2 — K-way merge: initialise a heap with one element from each of k sorted sources. Extract min, push next from that source. Repeat. Problems: Merge K Sorted Lists, Sort Matrix Diagonally, Find K-th Smallest in Matrix. Pattern 3 — Running statistics: maintain one or two heaps that update incrementally as new data arrives. Problems: Find Median from Data Stream (two heaps), Sliding Window Median (two heaps + lazy deletion). The heap type selection rule: for k-largest, use min-heap (you want to eject the smallest quickly). For k-smallest, use max-heap (eject the largest). The heap top is always the boundary between 'kept' and 'ejected'.
lessons.analogy: The three heap patterns are three different queue management strategies. Top-K is the VIP bouncer: maintain exactly k VIPs, eject the least special when a more special arrival comes. K-way merge is the traffic coordinator: manage k lanes and always process the car at the front of the queue with the lowest timestamp. Running statistics is the live scoreboard: update the running score as each new result arrives without recomputing from scratch.

code_example.explanation: Seven Blind 75 problems are covered in Module 9. All seven map directly to one of the three patterns. The pattern recognition exercise: read the problem signal, identify the pattern, select the heap type, state the time complexity before writing a line of code. This 60-second pattern identification is what separates candidates who have internalised heap thinking from those who have memorised specific solutions.

common_mistakes: Using a min-heap when a max-heap is needed or vice versa — memorise the rule: top-K largest needs a min-heap (eject smallest), top-K smallest needs a max-heap (eject largest); the heap type is always the opposite of what you want to keep

Using a heap when sorting is simpler for the given constraints — if n is small (< 100), k is close to n, or the problem is called once (not streaming), arr.sort() is cleaner with no practical performance difference
Not stating the O(n log k) time complexity unprompted — always state both the time and space complexity for heap solutions; many candidates say 'O(n)' forgetting the log k factor from heap operations
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 9 completes the foundational data structures in Level 1. Seven Blind 75 problems with heap solutions means this module alone covers a significant portion of any company's interview problem bank. Solving all seven fluently, stating the correct time/space complexity, and explaining the pattern selection for each is the measurable outcome of this module.

flashcards.front: Heap type rule for top-K: which heap for which goal?
flashcards.back: k LARGEST → MIN-heap (eject smallest). k SMALLEST → MAX-heap (eject largest). The heap type is always OPPOSITE to what you want to keep. The heap root is the boundary element.

flashcards.front: When does a heap beat sorting?
flashcards.back: When: k << n (top-k), streaming (data arrives one at a time), or repeated queries (maintain state across insertions). Sorting wins when: small n, need full sorted output, one-time query.

flashcards.front: K-way merge heap size throughout the algorithm?
flashcards.back: Always ≤ k (one element per non-exhausted source). Starts at k, decreases as sources are exhausted. Never grows beyond k.

flashcards.back: One heap can only give you O(1) access to its minimum or maximum. The median requires access to BOTH the maximum of the lower half AND the minimum of the upper half. Two heaps, each providing their extreme in O(1).

coding_challenges.problem_statement: Build a heap pattern classifier and demonstrate one representative solver from each of the three main heap patterns.
requirements: Implement `classifyHeapPattern(signals)` returning 'Top-K', 'K-Way Merge', or 'Running Statistics' based on signal words
Implement `solveTopK(nums, k)` — kth largest using min-heap (Top-K pattern)
Implement `solveKWayMerge(sortedArrays)` — merge k sorted arrays returning a single sorted array (K-way merge pattern)
Implement `solveRunningMedian(stream)` — return array of running medians after each insertion (Running Statistics pattern)
Implement `moduleCapabilitySummary()` confirming all three pattern solvers work

test_cases.input: (() => { const s = moduleCapabilitySummary(); return s.topK && s.kWayMerge && s.runningMedian; })()

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: classifyHeapPattern: O(1). solveTopK: O(n log k). solveKWayMerge: O(N log k). solveRunningMedian: O(n log n) total (O(log n) per insertion).

hints.text: classifyHeapPattern: map signal keywords to the three pattern names.
solveKWayMerge: k-way merge on arrays using binary-insert sorted-array simulation; same pattern as mergeKListsImpl but with array index tracking instead of node.next.
solveRunningMedian: two heaps with negation trick; after each addNum + rebalance, append the current median to the medians array.

core_patterns: Top-K with fixed-size min-heap (k largest) or max-heap (k smallest) — O(n log k)
K-way merge: heap of k current heads, push next on each extraction — O(N log k)
Running stats: max-heap lower half + min-heap upper half, rebalance on insert — O(log n) insert O(1) median
Heap type rule: opposite of what you keep (k-largest → min-heap, k-smallest → max-heap)
Squared distance optimisation: avoid sqrt for comparison-only use cases
Greedy + max-heap: Task Scheduler — always execute most frequent available task
Heapify O(n): bottom-up sift-down from index n/2 to 1, beats n×insert O(n log n)
Bucket sort for bounded-integer frequency problems: O(n) beats O(n log k)
Dummy head + heap tiebreaker index for stable multi-source merge
Global timestamp counter for total ordering in Design Twitter
